q: Which amino acid is achiral?
e: Glycine's side chain is a hydrogen, so its alpha carbon has two identical groups and is not a stereocenter.

q: Which amino acid has a side chain that is positively charged at physiological pH (7.4)?
e: Lysine's side-chain amine (pKa ≈ 10.5) is protonated at pH 7.4. Histidine's side chain (pKa ≈ 6) is mostly neutral at 7.4, and aspartate is negative.

q: An amino acid has pKa values of 2.3 (carboxyl) and 9.7 (amino) and no ionizable side chain. What is its isoelectric point?
e: For an amino acid with no charged side chain, pI is the average of the two pKa values: (2.3 + 9.7) / 2 = 6.0.

q: Which amino acid can form disulfide bonds?
e: Two cysteine thiol (–SH) groups can be oxidized to form a covalent S–S bridge. Methionine contains sulfur but as a thioether, which can't form disulfides.

q: Which amino acid is most likely to break an α-helix?
e: Proline's side chain loops back to its own backbone nitrogen, which makes it rigid and leaves no N–H to donate a hydrogen bond.

q: The α-helices and β-pleated sheets of a protein are held together mainly by:
a: Hydrogen bonds between backbone carbonyl and amide groups
w: Disulfide bonds between cysteine side chains on nearby strands
Hydrophobic interactions between nonpolar side chains in the core
Ionic bonds between oppositely charged side chains along the chain
e: Secondary structure comes from backbone hydrogen bonding. Side-chain interactions shape tertiary structure.

q: What drives a globular protein to fold with its hydrophobic side chains buried in the core?
a: An increase in the entropy of the surrounding water
w: Covalent bonds between hydrophobic side chains
A decrease in the protein's enthalpy only
The energy released by ATP hydrolysis
e: Exposed nonpolar groups force water into ordered cages. Burying them frees those water molecules, raising entropy (the hydrophobic effect).

q: Hemoglobin is made of four polypeptide subunits. The arrangement of these subunits is its:
e: Quaternary structure describes how multiple chains fit together. Single-chain proteins like myoglobin have no quaternary structure.

q: Urea and heat denature a protein. Which level of structure stays intact?
e: Denaturation disrupts noncovalent interactions but leaves the peptide bonds, and therefore the amino acid sequence, intact.

q: A competitive inhibitor affects an enzyme's kinetics by:
a: Raising the apparent Km while leaving Vmax unchanged
w: Lowering Vmax while leaving the apparent Km unchanged
Lowering both the apparent Km and Vmax by the same factor
Raising Vmax while lowering the apparent Km of the enzyme
e: The inhibitor competes for the active site, so more substrate is needed for half-maximal speed. Enough substrate outcompetes it, so Vmax is still reachable.

q: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds equally well to the free enzyme and to the enzyme–substrate complex. It will:
e: It removes active enzyme from play regardless of substrate, so Vmax falls. Because it doesn't change substrate binding, Km is unchanged.

q: On a Lineweaver–Burk (double-reciprocal) plot, the y-intercept equals:
e: The plot is 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax. The x-intercept is −1/Km and the slope is Km/Vmax.

q: An enzyme has a lower Km for substrate X than for substrate Y. This means the enzyme:
a: Has a higher apparent affinity for X
w: Has a higher apparent affinity for Y
Works faster on X at all concentrations
e: Km is the substrate concentration giving half of Vmax. Reaching it at a lower concentration suggests tighter binding.

q: Which statement about enzymes is FALSE?
a: They shift the equilibrium of the reactions they catalyze
w: They lower the activation energy of the reactions they speed up
They are not consumed or permanently changed by the reaction
They can be regulated by allosteric effectors and phosphorylation
e: Enzymes speed up both directions equally, so equilibrium is reached faster but the equilibrium constant is unchanged.

q: An allosteric enzyme shows a sigmoidal plot of velocity against substrate concentration. This shape indicates:
w: Competitive inhibition by the product of the reaction
Simple Michaelis–Menten kinetics with a single binding site
That each of the enzyme's subunits binds substrate independently
e: Binding at one site increases affinity at the others, just as with oxygen binding to hemoglobin.

q: Zymogens like pepsinogen and trypsinogen are made inactive mainly so that they:
a: Do not digest the cells that make them
w: Can cross the cell membrane more easily
Are more stable at low pH
e: These proteases are activated only after secretion. For example, enteropeptidase in the small intestine converts trypsinogen to trypsin.

q: Compared with hemoglobin, myoglobin's oxygen dissociation curve is:
a: Hyperbolic, with higher affinity for O₂ at low partial pressures
w: Sigmoidal, with lower affinity for O₂ at low partial pressures
Sigmoidal, with higher affinity for O₂ only at high partial pressures
Hyperbolic, with lower affinity for O₂ at every partial pressure
e: Myoglobin has one subunit and no cooperativity. It binds O₂ tightly, so it can take oxygen from hemoglobin in muscle.

q: Which change shifts hemoglobin's O₂ dissociation curve to the right?
a: Higher CO₂, lower pH and higher temperature
w: Lower CO₂, higher pH and lower temperature
e: A right shift means lower affinity, which unloads more O₂ in active tissues. CO₂, H⁺ (the Bohr effect), heat and 2,3-BPG all cause it.

q: G protein–coupled receptors are activated when a ligand binds and the associated G protein:
a: Exchanges GDP for GTP on its α subunit
e: The active Gα–GTP dissociates and regulates targets such as adenylyl cyclase, which then converts ATP to cAMP.

q: Which base pair is held together by three hydrogen bonds?
e: G–C pairs form three hydrogen bonds and A–T pairs form two, so GC-rich DNA melts at a higher temperature.

q: DNA polymerase adds new nucleotides only to which end of a growing strand?
w: The end closest to the origin
e: Polymerases need a free 3′-OH to attack the incoming nucleotide, so synthesis runs 5′ → 3′.

q: Why are Okazaki fragments formed during DNA replication?
a: Polymerase only works 5′ → 3′, so the lagging strand is made in pieces
w: Topoisomerase repeatedly nicks the leading strand as the fork advances
Helicase can only unwind short stretches, so both strands are copied in pieces
Primase lays down primers on both strands, which blocks continuous synthesis
e: The lagging strand runs the opposite way from fork movement, so it is built in short pieces that ligase later joins.

q: Which enzyme relieves the supercoiling that builds up ahead of the replication fork?
e: Helicase unwinds the double helix, which overwinds the DNA ahead of it. Topoisomerases cut and rejoin strands to release that strain.

q: DNA replication is described as semiconservative because:
a: Each new double helix contains one original strand and one new strand
w: Half of the genome is copied during each round of the cell cycle
Only one of the two strands is copied, and the other is conserved
Both original strands end up together in the same daughter cell
e: This was shown by the Meselson–Stahl experiment using heavy and light nitrogen isotopes.

q: In eukaryotes, which modification is NOT part of processing pre-mRNA into mature mRNA?
e: The Shine–Dalgarno sequence is a prokaryotic ribosome-binding site. Eukaryotic mRNA is capped, polyadenylated and spliced.

q: Which eukaryotic RNA polymerase transcribes protein-coding genes into mRNA?
e: Pol I makes most rRNA, Pol II makes mRNA (and some small RNAs), and Pol III makes tRNA and 5S rRNA.

q: Alternative splicing allows one gene to:
a: Encode several different proteins by including different exons
w: Be transcribed by several different RNA polymerases
Be translated starting from several different start codons
Skip transcription and be translated directly from DNA
e: By combining exons differently, a cell can make several protein variants (isoforms) from a single gene.

q: A tRNA anticodon reads 5′-CAU-3′. Which mRNA codon does it pair with?
e: Pairing is antiparallel. Matching the anticodon's 3′ U with A, A with U and 5′ C with G gives the codon 5′-AUG-3′ (methionine, the start codon).

q: Which is a stop codon?
e: The three stop codons are UAA, UAG and UGA. AUG is the start codon, and UGG codes for tryptophan.

q: A peptide bond forms when the growing chain is transferred onto the amino acid in which ribosomal site?
e: The incoming aminoacyl-tRNA enters the A site. Peptidyl transferase (rRNA in the large subunit) moves the chain from the P-site tRNA onto it.

q: The genetic code is called degenerate because:
a: Most amino acids are specified by more than one codon
w: Some codons code for more than one amino acid in different cells
Codons can overlap with each other within a single reading frame
It differs widely between species, so each needs its own codon table
e: There are 61 sense codons for 20 amino acids. The code is redundant but unambiguous: each codon specifies only one amino acid.

q: A single base deletion in the middle of a gene's coding sequence most likely causes:
a: A frameshift that changes all downstream codons
w: No change, because of the degenerate code
e: Deleting a number of bases that isn't a multiple of 3 shifts the reading frame and often creates an early stop codon.

q: A point mutation changes a codon for an amino acid into a stop codon. This is called a:
e: Nonsense mutations end translation early and usually produce a shortened, nonfunctional protein.

q: In the lac operon, when lactose is present and glucose is absent:
a: The repressor is released, CAP–cAMP binds, and transcription is high
w: The repressor stays bound to the operator, so transcription remains off
CAP–cAMP is released from the promoter, so transcription stays low
The repressor and CAP–cAMP both bind and block RNA polymerase together
e: Allolactose pulls the repressor off the operator. Low glucose raises cAMP, and CAP–cAMP helps RNA polymerase bind for strong transcription.

q: Histone acetylation generally:
w: Adds methyl groups to cytosines in DNA
e: Acetyl groups neutralize lysines' positive charges, which weakens histone binding to negatively charged DNA.

q: In eukaryotes, DNA methylation at CpG sites in a promoter usually:
e: Methylated promoters attract proteins that compact chromatin and block transcription factors. This is a common way to silence genes epigenetically.

q: In PCR, the annealing step happens at a moderate temperature (about 55 °C) so that:
a: Primers can bind to complementary sequences on the single strands
w: The hydrogen bonds between the two template strands break apart
Taq polymerase can extend new strands at its optimal temperature
Newly made fragments can be sealed together by heat-stable DNA ligase
e: PCR cycles through denaturation (about 95 °C), annealing (about 50–65 °C) and extension (about 72 °C).

q: Reverse transcriptase is used to make cDNA libraries because it:
a: Builds DNA from an mRNA template, giving sequences without introns
w: Copies genomic DNA into RNA, keeping the introns in place
Cuts genomic DNA at palindromic sites into gene-sized pieces
Joins mRNA molecules end to end into a single long strand
e: cDNA comes from processed mRNA, so it lacks introns. That lets eukaryotic genes be expressed in bacteria, which can't splice.

q: Two heterozygous parents (Aa × Aa) have a child. What is the chance the child shows the recessive phenotype?
e: The cross gives 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa. Only aa shows the recessive trait.

q: In an AaBb × AaBb cross with independent assortment, what fraction of offspring show both recessive phenotypes?
e: (1/4 for aa) × (1/4 for bb) = 1/16. The classic dihybrid ratio is 9:3:3:1.

q: A mother who carries an X-linked recessive disorder has a son with an unaffected father. What is the probability the son is affected?
e: Sons get their only X from the mother. She passes the affected X half the time.

q: A cross between red and white snapdragons gives all pink offspring. This is an example of:
e: The heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype. In codominance, both traits show fully, as in AB blood type.

q: A person with type AB blood shows both A and B antigens on their red blood cells. This is an example of:
e: Both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote.

q: Crossing over between homologous chromosomes happens during:
e: Homologs pair into tetrads (synapsis) in prophase I and swap segments at chiasmata.

q: Homologous chromosomes separate during:
e: Meiosis I separates homologs (reductional division). Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, much like mitosis.

q: Nondisjunction during meiosis can produce trisomy 21. Nondisjunction means:
a: Chromosomes or chromatids fail to separate properly
w: A chromosome segment is reversed end to end
A gene is duplicated on the same chromosome
e: If a pair fails to separate, one gamete gets two copies and another gets none. Fertilization then gives a trisomy or monosomy.

q: Two genes are 20 map units apart. What percentage of offspring from a test cross are expected to be recombinant?
e: One map unit (centimorgan) equals 1% recombination frequency.

q: In a population in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, the recessive allele frequency is 0.3. What fraction of people are heterozygous?
e: p = 0.7 and q = 0.3. Heterozygotes are 2pq = 2 × 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.42.

q: A recessive disorder affects 1 in 10,000 people in a population in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium. About what fraction are carriers?
e: q² = 1/10,000, so q = 0.01 and p ≈ 0.99. Carriers = 2pq ≈ 0.02, or about 1 in 50.

q: Which condition is NOT required for Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium?
e: Hardy–Weinberg requires a very large population. In small populations, genetic drift changes allele frequencies by chance.

q: A small group colonizes an island, and its allele frequencies differ from the mainland population by chance. This is called:
e: The founder effect is a kind of genetic drift: a small sample from a larger population doesn't represent its genetic diversity.

q: The sickle-cell allele stays common in areas with malaria because heterozygotes resist malaria. This is an example of:
w: Directional selection for the sickle allele
e: Heterozygotes have higher fitness than either homozygote, which keeps both alleles in the population (balancing selection).

q: What is the net ATP yield of glycolysis per glucose molecule?
e: Glycolysis uses 2 ATP in the investment phase and makes 4 in the payoff phase. It also produces 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate.

q: Which enzyme catalyzes the main regulated, committed step of glycolysis?
e: PFK-1 converts fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. It is inhibited by ATP and citrate and activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate.

q: During intense exercise, muscle converts pyruvate to lactate mainly to:
a: Regenerate NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue
e: Without enough oxygen, the electron transport chain can't reoxidize NADH. Lactate dehydrogenase does it instead, keeping glycolysis going.

q: Where does the citric acid cycle take place in eukaryotic cells?
e: The only exception is succinate dehydrogenase, which is embedded in the inner membrane and doubles as Complex II of the electron transport chain.

q: One turn of the citric acid cycle produces:
a: 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP (or ATP) and 2 CO₂
w: 2 NADH, 2 FADH₂, 2 ATP (or GTP) and 1 CO₂
1 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 3 ATP (or GTP) and 2 CO₂
3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 3 ATP (or GTP) and no CO₂
e: Each glucose gives 2 acetyl-CoA, so the cycle turns twice per glucose.

q: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex converts pyruvate into:
e: This link reaction connects glycolysis to the citric acid cycle and happens in the mitochondrial matrix.

q: What is the final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain?
e: Complex IV passes electrons to O₂, which picks up protons to form water.

q: ATP synthase makes ATP using energy from:
a: Protons flowing from the intermembrane space back into the matrix
w: Electrons passing directly through ATP synthase from NADH to oxygen
Protons being pumped from the matrix out into the intermembrane space
GTP hydrolysis from substrate-level phosphorylation in the cycle
e: The electron transport chain pumps H⁺ out into the intermembrane space. Their return through ATP synthase drives its rotation (chemiosmosis).

q: An uncoupler such as 2,4-dinitrophenol makes the inner mitochondrial membrane leaky to protons. What happens?
a: Oxygen use rises, ATP production falls and more energy is lost as heat
w: Oxygen use stops, ATP production rises and less heat is released
Oxygen use falls, ATP production falls and less heat is released
Oxygen use rises, ATP production rises and the gradient grows larger
e: The proton gradient leaks away, so electron transport runs fast to try to rebuild it, but ATP synthase is bypassed. Brown fat uses a natural uncoupler (thermogenin) to make heat.

q: Cyanide is lethal because it:
a: Blocks Complex IV, stopping electron flow to oxygen
w: Blocks hexokinase, which stops glycolysis in every cell
Makes the inner membrane leaky to protons, wasting the gradient
Binds the ATP synthase rotor and stops it from turning
e: With Complex IV blocked, the whole chain backs up, the proton gradient collapses and aerobic ATP production stops.

q: In the fasting state, which hormone stimulates the liver to break down glycogen and make new glucose?
e: Glucagon from pancreatic α-cells raises blood glucose through glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. Insulin does the opposite.

q: Gluconeogenesis bypasses three irreversible steps of glycolysis. Which enzyme bypasses pyruvate kinase together with PEP carboxykinase?
e: Pyruvate carboxylase turns pyruvate into oxaloacetate in the mitochondria. PEPCK then converts oxaloacetate into phosphoenolpyruvate.

q: Fatty acid β-oxidation takes place in the:
e: Long-chain fatty acids enter the mitochondria via the carnitine shuttle. Each round of β-oxidation removes two carbons as acetyl-CoA. Fatty acid synthesis happens in the cytosol.

q: During prolonged starvation, the liver produces ketone bodies mainly to:
a: Provide an alternate fuel for the brain and other tissues
w: Store excess glucose as a compact fuel reserve
Convert fatty acids back into new glucose molecules
Raise blood pH to counter acid from muscle breakdown
e: With glucose scarce, acetyl-CoA from fat breakdown becomes ketone bodies (acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate), which the brain can adapt to use.

q: The pentose phosphate pathway's main products are:
e: NADPH supports biosynthesis and protects against oxidative damage. Ribose-5-phosphate is used to make nucleotides.

q: Under cellular conditions, ATP hydrolysis can drive an unfavorable reaction because:
a: Coupling the two reactions makes the overall ΔG negative
w: ATP lowers the activation energy of the unfavorable reaction
ATP hydrolysis has a positive ΔG
The unfavorable reaction becomes favorable at high temperature
e: ΔG values add for coupled reactions. ATP hydrolysis releases enough free energy to make the overall process spontaneous.
